The AD requires the forward-engine-mount inspection to be performed using the updated inspection intervals specified in the 737MAX_CMM_Engine_Mount document, which were revised to comply with FAA-AD-2024-01-02. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2022-03-07.
Southwest Airlines is listed as an operator linked to the Boeing 737 MAX, and therefore is affected by the MCAS software requirements.

The FAA, as the primary certification authority, issues Airworthiness Directives (e.g., AD 2020-05-11, AD 2022-03-07, AD 2024-01-02) that require inspection and maintenance of the LEAP-1B engine mount. Those ADs reference manufacturer documents-Boeing Service Bulletin 737-31-1887 rev1 and CFM AD CFM-2023-14-which specify the exact procedures the maintenance crew must perform. The crew then carries out the inspections and corrective actions, as shown by G-ABCD’s compliance records for the FAA ADs and the CFM AD.

Southwest’s 87 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft were grounded on 13 Mar 2019 by the FAA Emergency Order, then returned to revenue service on 11 Mar 2021 after satisfying FAA AD 2020-05-11 (compliant by Nov 2020). The fleet also met the enhanced AOA-monitoring requirements of FAA AD 2022-03-07 (compliant by Apr 2022). It is still pending compliance with FAA AD 2024-01-02, which mandates installation of MCAS software v2.0 (Boeing Service Bulletin 737-31-1944 Rev2) no later than 15 May 2024; Southwest has scheduled the upgrades from Feb-May 2024 at roughly ten aircraft per month.

The 2022 AD (AD 2022-03-07) partially superseded the 2020 AD (AD 2020-05-11) and is itself superseded by the 2024 AD (AD 2024-01-02). Thus the 2022 directive updated the return-to-service and AOA-monitoring requirements introduced in 2020, but those requirements are now replaced by the newer MCAS-v2.0 mandate in the 2024 AD. For operators, this means the 2022 AD must already be complied with (most fleets are listed as compliant), but they must now transition to the 2024 AD’s requirements and meet its May 15 2024 compliance deadline, while the original 2020 AD obligations remain satisfied but are incorporated into the newer rule.

No. G-ABCD meets FAA AD 2020-05-11 and FAA AD 2022-03-07, but it is IS_NON_COMPLIANT_WITH FAA AD 2024-01-02, which mandates MCAS v2.0 installation by the May 15 2024 deadline. The March 2024 compliance report flags this pending requirement. Consequently, the aircraft is not fully compliant with all applicable FAA MCAS ADs as of March 2024. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2020-05-11, FAA-AD-2022-03-07, FAA-AD-2024-01-02.

No. In March 2024 G-ABCD was still considered airworthy because the FAA AD 2024-01-02 compliance deadline (May 15 2024) had not yet passed, and the report explicitly states the aircraft remains airworthy until that deadline despite the current non-compliance. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2024-01-02.
The current governing document for Boeing 737 MAX engine-mount inspection is the **737MAX_CMM_Engine_Mount** manual, **rev12** (dated Nov 2023).

No. FAA-AD-2020-05-11 has been superseded-partially by AD 2022-03-07 and fully by AD 2024-01-02-so it is no longer the governing airworthiness directive. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2022-03-07, FAA-AD-2024-01-02.

The regulatory chain starts with **14 CFR Part 39**, which gives the FAA authority to issue Airworthiness Directives. Those directives-**FAA-AD-2020-05-11**, **FAA-AD-2022-03-07**, and **FAA-AD-2024-01-02**-specify the required engine-mount and sensor-bracket inspections for 737-8/-9 aircraft. The ADs in turn reference the **Boeing Service Bulletin 737-31-1710**, the **CFM AD CFM-2023-14**, and the detailed procedures in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (e.g., AMM Task 71-21-05 Rev12). Boeing’s FAA Production Approval and Design Approval Holder status under **Parts 21, 25, and 39** underpins the whole compliance framework.

Yes. The context states that AD 2020-05-11 is “fully superseded by this AD” (FAA-AD-2024-01-02). This indicates that the 2024 directive replaces the 2020 directive even though the two documents do not directly cite each other. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2020-05-11.

Yes. FAA-AD-2024-01-02 applies to Boeing Model 737-8 and 737-9 airplanes, and Southwest Airlines is a primary U.S. operator of the 737 MAX fleet. Under 14 CFR Part 39, operators of those models must comply with all applicable ADs, including AD 2024-01-02. Therefore Southwest Airlines is required to meet the directive’s requirements. Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2020-05-11, FAA-AD-2022-03-07.

MCAS Software version 2.0 is the current version. It supersedes v1.7.3 and earlier releases and is required by FAA AD 2024-01-02.

Three FAA airworthiness directives were issued between 2020 and 2024 that pertain to the 737 MAX engine mount: AD 2020-05-11, AD 2022-03-07 (which includes forward-pylon/engine-mount inspection), and AD 2024-01-02 (which updates inspection intervals for the mount). Relevant FAA directives in the retrieved evidence: FAA-AD-2020-05-11, FAA-AD-2022-03-07, FAA-AD-2024-01-02.

The FAA, as the primary certification authority, issues airworthiness directives such as FAA AD 2024-01-02, FAA AD 2022-03-07, and FAA AD 2020-05-11 that govern continued airworthiness of the LEAP-1B engine mount and related structures on Boeing 737-8 aircraft. British Horizon Airways, the aircraft operator, must satisfy those ADs, and the required inspections are carried out by its base-maintenance provider, SR Technics in Zurich, during the C-Check documented in the G-ABCD inspection report. SR Technics follows the Boeing 737-MAX CMM Engine Mount chapter rev12 (dated Nov 15 2023) and verifies compliance with the FAA ADs, recording the work as “IS_COMPLIANT_WITH” in the aircraft’s AD compliance status. Thus the regulatory chain runs: FAA → issued ADs → operator → maintenance crew (SR Technics) → inspection/compliance actions on the CFM LEAP-1B engine.
The provided context does not contain sufficient information to explain the compliance chain from FAA-AD-2024 to Southwest Airlines’ 737 MAX fleet.

14 CFR Part 39 governs airworthiness directives, the legally enforceable rules that require inspections, limitations, and corrective actions to address unsafe conditions in aircraft, engines, propellers, and appliances. The FAA Airworthiness Directive 2022-03-07 (AD 2022-03-07) cites 14 CFR Part 39.

The EASA AD 2024-0072 applies to the Airbus A320neo family, specifically the A320-200N (including the A320-271N) and the A321-271N series. It covers only those airplanes that are equipped with Flight Management and Guidance Computer software standard P/12C or an earlier version.
